Last week's impeachment articles against US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth neatly highlight how much damage the Trump administration has done to American "exceptionalism" and to US foreign policy generally. And there are lessons for Australia here.

Login or signup to continue reading

Critically, Hegseth was accused of illegally waging and continuing military hostilities against Iran for more than 90 days in violation of the War Powers Resolution and without congressional authorisation.

The 240-year-old US Constitution gives the power to declare war exclusively to Congress. That was part of the post-revolutionary package that made the United States exceptional - different from Europe.

For centuries, European monarchs waged war against each other, dragging their people into loss of blood and treasure without their consent. The monarchs often made alliances to fight these wars, making them even bloodier.

The United States was to be different. It was to be governed, not ruled, and governed with the consent of those being governed. Only the people's representatives in Congress could wage war. And treaties (usually the vehicle for alliances) had to be approved by two-thirds of the Senate.

After World War I, the war to end all wars, the US, under president Woodrow Wilson, embarked on a mission to do just that by creating the League of Nations that would outlaw all but defensive wars. Wilson was dismissed as an impractical idealist, the Senate rejected the League of Nations, and without the US at the forefront of world affairs, the League was unable to prevent World War II.

After World War II, the US was determined not to repeat the errors of the 1930s. The United Nations, which was shaped by President Franklin Roosevelt and Winston Churchill, became a key element of US foreign policy.

Critically, UN rules permitted armed conflict only in self-defence, or helping another nation's self-defence, or with UN approval. The primary aim of US foreign policy was to support democracy and freedom against tyranny and autocracy. It would defend those attacked.
